title: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Systems that learn patterns from data to predict, generate and act.
hook: Rules are a recipe you write; ML is tasting thousands of dishes and inferring the recipe.

cards.q: In one sentence, how does machine learning differ from hand-written rules?
cards.a: Rules are written by hand; ML infers the rules from examples by minimizing error on data.

cards.q: Name the three big learning paradigms.
cards.a: Supervised (labeled examples), unsupervised (find structure without labels), reinforcement (learn from reward by acting).

children.title: ML Foundations
children.summary: Data, models, loss and optimization: the loop under every learned system.
children.hook: Every ML system is the same loop: guess, measure how wrong, nudge, repeat.

cards.q: What are the four ingredients of a supervised learning setup?
cards.a: Data, a model (parameterized function), a loss function, and an optimizer.

cards.q: Why do we hold out a test set?
cards.a: To estimate performance on unseen data; scoring on training data rewards memorization.

children.title: Supervised Learning
children.summary: Learn a mapping from inputs to labeled outputs: regression and classification.
children.hook: A student with an answer key: practice problems plus the right answers.

cards.q: Give one regression and one classification example.
cards.a: Regression: predict house price. Classification: spam or not spam.

cards.q: What is a label?
cards.a: The correct output paired with an input, the 'answer' the model learns to predict.

children.title: Loss Functions
children.summary: A number that says how wrong the model is; training makes it smaller.
children.hook: Loss is the golf score: lower is better, and training is practicing to shave strokes.

cards.q: When would you use cross-entropy instead of mean squared error?
cards.a: Classification with probabilities: cross-entropy punishes confident wrong answers hard; MSE suits continuous targets.

cards.q: What does the loss surface look like conceptually?
cards.a: A landscape over parameter space where height is error; training walks downhill.

children.title: Gradient Descent
children.summary: Step parameters opposite the gradient of the loss, scaled by a learning rate.
children.hook: Walking down a foggy mountain by feeling which way the ground slopes under your feet.

cards.q: What happens if the learning rate is too large?
cards.a: It overshoots the valley, bouncing around or diverging instead of settling.

cards.q: Why is it called stochastic gradient descent when we use mini-batches?
cards.a: Each step uses a random small batch, so the gradient is a noisy (stochastic) estimate of the true one.

children.title: Overfitting & Generalization
children.summary: Doing well on unseen data, not just memorizing the training set.
children.hook: Memorizing last year's exam answers vs understanding the subject.

cards.q: Name two signs of overfitting.
cards.a: Training loss keeps dropping while validation loss rises; huge gap between train and test accuracy.

cards.q: Name three ways to reduce it.
cards.a: More data, regularization (weight decay, dropout), early stopping, simpler model, data augmentation.

children.title: Neural Networks
children.summary: Stacks of linear layers and nonlinearities trained end to end with backpropagation.
children.hook: Lego: simple identical bricks (linear + bend) stacked deep enough build any shape.

cards.q: Why does a network need nonlinear activations?
cards.a: Without them, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear function, so depth adds nothing.

cards.q: What is a layer, concretely?
cards.a: A matrix multiply plus bias (Wx + b) followed by an elementwise activation.

children.title: Neurons & Layers
children.summary: Weighted sum plus bias, passed through an activation; many in parallel form a layer.
children.hook: A neuron is a voter: weigh each input's opinion, add a bias, then decide how loudly to speak.

cards.q: Write the formula for one neuron.
cards.a: y = f(w · x + b).

cards.q: What does a layer's weight matrix shape mean?
cards.a: W is (outputs × inputs): each row is one neuron's weights over all inputs.

children.title: Activation Functions
children.summary: ReLU, GELU, sigmoid, tanh: the nonlinearities that make depth useful.
children.hook: Activations are the bends in a wire; without bends you can only make straight lines.

cards.q: Why did ReLU replace sigmoid in deep nets?
cards.a: ReLU doesn't saturate for positive inputs, so gradients stay strong; it's also cheap to compute.

cards.q: What is the vanishing gradient problem?
cards.a: Gradients shrink as they multiply through many saturating layers, so early layers barely learn.

children.title: Backpropagation
children.summary: The chain rule applied layer by layer to get gradients for every weight.
children.hook: Blame assignment: pass the error backward, each layer takes its share of the blame.

cards.q: Explain backprop in two sentences.
cards.a: Run forward to get the loss, then apply the chain rule from the output back, reusing each layer's gradient for the one before it.

cards.q: Why compute gradients backward instead of forward?
cards.a: One backward pass gets gradients for all weights at once because the loss is a single scalar; forward mode would need a pass per parameter.

children.title: Convolutional Nets
children.summary: Shared local filters that exploit spatial structure in images.
children.hook: A flashlight sliding over the image, looking for the same pattern everywhere.

cards.q: What does weight sharing buy you?
cards.a: Far fewer parameters and translation equivariance: a cat-ear detector works anywhere in the image.

cards.q: What does pooling do?
cards.a: Downsamples feature maps, keeping the strongest signals and adding small shift invariance.

children.title: Transformers
children.summary: Attention-based architecture behind modern language, vision and audio models.
children.hook: A meeting where every word can talk to every other word at once, instead of a game of telephone.

cards.q: What problem with RNNs did transformers solve?
cards.a: RNNs process tokens one by one, so they're slow to train and forget long-range context; attention is parallel and direct.

cards.q: Name the main blocks of a transformer layer.
cards.a: Multi-head self-attention, a feed-forward MLP, with residual connections and layer norm around each.

children.title: Tokenization
children.summary: Splitting text into subword tokens (BPE) the model maps to embeddings.
children.hook: Lego bricks for text: common words are one brick, rare words snap together from pieces.

cards.q: Why subwords instead of whole words or characters?
cards.a: Words leave too many rare/unknown items; characters make sequences very long. Subwords balance vocabulary and length.

cards.q: Why can token counts differ between languages?
cards.a: Tokenizers are trained mostly on some languages, so others split into many more pieces per word.

children.title: Embeddings
children.summary: Dense vectors for tokens; similar meanings land near each other.
children.hook: A map where meaning is location: 'king' and 'queen' live in the same neighborhood.

cards.q: What is an embedding table?
cards.a: A learned matrix with one row (vector) per token id; lookup replaces one-hot multiplication.

cards.q: How is cosine similarity used with embeddings?
cards.a: The angle between vectors measures similarity, used for search, retrieval and clustering.

children.title: Self-Attention
children.summary: Each token mixes information from others, weighted by query-key similarity.
children.hook: A library: your query is matched against every book's key, and you read a blend of the best-matching values.

cards.q: Write softmax(QK^T/√d)V and explain each part.
cards.a: Q·Kᵀ scores how relevant each token is to each other token, √d keeps scores in range, softmax turns them into weights, and the weights average V.

cards.q: Why scale by √d?
cards.a: Dot products grow with dimension d; without scaling, softmax saturates and gradients vanish.

cards.q: What does multi-head add?
cards.a: Several attention patterns in parallel, each free to focus on a different relationship (syntax, coreference, position).

children.title: Positional Encoding
children.summary: Injecting token order, since attention alone is order-blind (sinusoidal, RoPE).
children.hook: Attention sees a bag of words; position encoding stamps each word with a seat number.

cards.q: Why does attention need position information?
cards.a: Attention is permutation-invariant: shuffle the tokens and the scores are the same, so order must be injected.

cards.q: What does RoPE rotate?
cards.a: The query and key vectors, by an angle proportional to position, so their dot product depends on relative distance.

children.title: Large Language Models
children.summary: Transformers pretrained on huge text corpora to predict the next token, then tuned to be useful.
children.hook: Autocomplete trained on the internet, then coached to be a helpful assistant.

cards.q: What is the pretraining objective of a GPT-style model?
cards.a: Predict the next token given all previous ones (causal language modeling).

cards.q: What changes between a base model and a chat model?
cards.a: A chat model is further tuned on instructions and human preferences to follow requests and hold a conversation.

children.title: Pretraining & Scaling
children.summary: Next-token prediction at scale; loss falls predictably with data, params and compute.
children.hook: Bigger brain, more books, more study time: loss falls on a smooth, predictable curve.

cards.q: State the gist of scaling laws.
cards.a: Loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute, so you can predict gains before training.

cards.q: Why does next-token prediction teach so much?
cards.a: To predict the next word well you must model grammar, facts, reasoning and intent, so those skills emerge.

children.title: Fine-tuning & RLHF
children.summary: Instruction tuning and preference optimization to make models helpful and safe.
children.hook: Pretraining is reading the library; fine-tuning is the apprenticeship that teaches manners and the job.

cards.q: What data does instruction tuning use?
cards.a: Pairs of instructions and high-quality responses, often written or curated by humans.

cards.q: What does the reward model in RLHF learn?
cards.a: To score responses the way humans would prefer, learned from pairwise human comparisons.

children.title: Prompting
children.summary: Steering a model with instructions, examples and structure in the context window.
children.hook: Briefing a brilliant new contractor: context, examples and the format you want.

cards.q: What is few-shot prompting?
cards.a: Including a few input→output examples in the prompt so the model infers the task.

cards.q: Why does asking for step-by-step reasoning help?
cards.a: It gives the model room to compute intermediate steps in tokens instead of jumping to an answer.

children.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
children.summary: Fetch relevant documents and put them in context so answers are grounded.
children.hook: An open-book exam: look up the relevant pages, then answer.

cards.q: Sketch the RAG pipeline in four steps.
cards.a: Chunk and embed documents → embed the query and retrieve nearest chunks → put them in the prompt → generate a grounded answer.

cards.q: When is RAG better than fine-tuning?
cards.a: When facts change often, must be cited, or are private; fine-tuning is better for teaching style or skills.

children.title: Agents & Tool Use
children.summary: Models that call tools in a loop to act, observe and plan toward a goal.
children.hook: A model with hands: think, use a tool, look at the result, repeat.

cards.q: What is a tool call, mechanically?
cards.a: The model outputs a structured request (name + arguments); the host runs it and returns the result as new input.

cards.q: Name two failure modes of agent loops.
cards.a: Looping without progress, and compounding errors from a bad early step or a misread tool result.

children.title: Reinforcement Learning
children.summary: Learning by trial and error to maximize reward from an environment.
children.hook: Training a dog: no answer key, just treats for good outcomes.

cards.q: Define agent, environment, state, action and reward.
cards.a: Agent acts; environment responds; state is the situation; action is the choice; reward is the score signal.

cards.q: What is the exploration-exploitation tradeoff?
cards.a: Exploit what you know pays off, or explore to find something better.

children.title: Markov Decision Processes
children.summary: The formal frame: states, actions, transitions, rewards and a discount factor.
children.hook: A board game: where you stand now is all you need to know to play the next move.

cards.q: What does the Markov property say?
cards.a: The future depends only on the current state and action, not on how you got there.

cards.q: What does the discount factor γ control?
cards.a: How much future rewards count compared to immediate ones; γ near 1 is far-sighted.

children.title: Q-Learning
children.summary: Learn the value of each action in each state from bootstrapped targets.
children.hook: A cheat sheet scoring every move in every position, refined after each game.

cards.q: Write the Q-learning update rule.
cards.a: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ·maxₐ' Q(s',a') − Q(s,a)].

cards.q: What did DQN add to make it work with images?
cards.a: A neural network for Q, an experience replay buffer, and a slowly updated target network.

children.title: Policy Gradients
children.summary: Directly adjust a policy's parameters toward actions that earned more reward (REINFORCE, PPO).
children.hook: Do more of what just worked, less of what didn't, adjusted directly in the habit itself.

cards.q: Why do policy gradients have high variance?
cards.a: Returns from sampled episodes vary a lot, so the gradient estimate is noisy; baselines reduce this.

cards.q: What does PPO's clipping prevent?
cards.a: Too-large policy updates in one step that would wreck a working policy.

children.title: Evaluation & Safety
children.summary: Measuring what models can do and keeping their behavior within bounds.
children.hook: You can't improve what you can't measure, and you can't trust what you haven't stress-tested.

cards.q: Why are static benchmarks not enough?
cards.a: They get saturated, leak into training data, and miss real-world behavior.

cards.q: Name two categories of AI risk.
cards.a: Misuse (people using it for harm) and misalignment (the model pursuing unintended goals).

children.title: Metrics
children.summary: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, perplexity: picking the number that matches the goal.
children.hook: Pick the scoreboard that matches the game you're actually playing.

cards.q: When is accuracy misleading?
cards.a: With imbalanced classes: 99% accuracy by always predicting 'not fraud.'

cards.q: Define precision and recall.
cards.a: Precision: of predicted positives, how many are right. Recall: of actual positives, how many you found.

children.title: LLM Evals
children.summary: Benchmarks, held-out tasks and model-graded evals for open-ended outputs.
children.hook: A test only measures what it hasn't already leaked into the textbook.

cards.q: What is benchmark contamination?
cards.a: Test questions appear in training data, inflating scores.

cards.q: What are the risks of LLM-as-judge?
cards.a: Judge bias (length, position, self-preference) and blind spots shared with the model under test.

children.title: Alignment & Safety
children.summary: Red-teaming, interpretability and guardrails against harmful or deceptive behavior.
children.hook: Seatbelts, crash tests and an X-ray of the engine.

cards.q: What is a jailbreak?
cards.a: A prompt that tricks a model into bypassing its safety behavior.

cards.q: What does interpretability research try to find?
cards.a: The internal features and circuits that explain how a model computes its outputs.
